forces: Alto, solo violin, strings and continuo
performers: Hertha Töpper, alto; Otto Büchner, solo violin; Münchener Bach-Orchester; Karl Richter, conductor
intro: After Peter’s denial, an alto asks for mercy while a solo violin sings beside her. Hertha Töpper and Otto Büchner share the lament in this aria from Karl Richter’s 1958 St Matthew Passion.

sections.label: A · The violin sings first
sections.mNote: A solo violin rises above soft strings and plucked bass

sections.label: B · The alto asks for mercy
sections.mNote: Erbarme dich enters after the violin’s fermata

sections.label: C · Violin, then Schaue hier
sections.mNote: A violin interlude separates the two parts of the poem

sections.label: B′ · Erbarme dich returns
sections.mNote: The opening plea returns in B minor

sections.label: A′ · The violin has the last word
sections.mNote: The opening violin music closes the aria

cues.title: A violin sings first
cues.text: The solo violin bends its long phrases over a gently rocking bass. Bach marks the accompanying strings piano sempre — softly throughout — and the bass pizzicato, plucked. The voice waits through eight bars of this B-minor music.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, vol. 4 (1854), Part II, printed p. 168: 12/8, solo violin, piano sempre strings and pizzicato continuo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d7/IMSLP00935-Bach_StMatt2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The alto asks for mercy
cues.text: “Erbarme dich, mein Gott” — “Have mercy, my God.” The alto enters after the violin’s held chord. Her phrases keep breaking off between appeals, while the violin rejoins her with a flowing line of its own.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 168–169: fermata ending the introduction, alto entry and solo violin rests before its answering phrases. Picander’s aria text, Leipzig, 1727.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Peter goes out weeping
cues.text: In the preceding recitative, Peter denies Jesus three times. The cock crows; Peter remembers the warning and goes out weeping. Picander’s aria carries the last word of that account into its own poem: “bitterlich”, bitterly. The alto’s grief grows from the narrator’s final sentence.
cues.evidence: Matthew 26:69–75 and Picander’s text for BWV 244, Nos. 38 and 39 in modern numbering. German text: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244.

cues.title: Bach with a violin
cues.text: In 1703 Bach spends half a year as a violinist in Duke Johann Ernst’s private orchestra at Weimar. He is eighteen. His next job is at the organ in Arnstadt; here, years later, he gives a violin the first and last word.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig chronology, 1703: violinist with Duke Johann Ernst III, then appointment at Arnstadt. https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology. Violin introduction and Dal Segno: Bach-Gesellschaft score, pp. 168 and 172.

cues.title: The violin fills the pause
cues.text: The alto ends “um meiner Zähren willen” — “for the sake of my tears” — and rests. The violin carries a short interlude in F♯ minor above the continuing bass. The next words, “Schaue hier”, begin the poem’s second thought: heart and eyes weep before God.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed p. 170: cadence in F♯ minor, violin interlude and entry on Schaue hier. Picander’s text is printed beneath the voice.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The music stands in the room
cues.text: In May 1959 the critic Heinrich Sievers reviews Richter’s four stereo LPs. Of the arias with solo instruments he writes that “the music is no longer projected but stands alive in the room”. Here Hertha Töpper sings, with Otto Büchner on solo violin.
cues.evidence: Deutsche Grammophon booklet for the 1958 recording (Internet Archive item, Booklet.pdf): Sievers, May 1959, “man hat den Eindruck, dass die Musik nicht mehr projiziert wird, sondern lebendig im Raum steht” (our translation); the booklet also credits Töpper with solo arias and Büchner as violinist. https://archive.org/details/munchener-bach-chor-munchener-bach-orchester-karl-richter-johann-sebastian-b

cues.title: The same plea returns
cues.text: After “bitterlich”, the alto calls “Erbarme dich” again. The opening plea gradually regains its B-minor home, and the violin resumes its curling phrases beside the voice. The words are few; Bach gives them room to be said over and over.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 171–172: repeated Erbarme dich after bitterlich, return to B minor and continuation of the solo violin part.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bach’s own score
cues.text: The aria survives in Bach’s own handwriting. His score of the revised Passion, written out between 1736 and 1740, is kept at the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin as Mus. ms. Bach P 25.
cues.evidence: IMSLP, St Matthew Passion page: holograph manuscript, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, Mus. ms. Bach P 25, dated 1736–40. https://imslp.org/wiki/St._Matthew_Passion,_BWV_244_(Bach,_Johann_Sebastian). Netherlands Bach Society: “Bach’s manuscript of 1736 has been handed down.” https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244

cues.title: The violin closes the aria
cues.text: The alto finishes “for the sake of my tears”. Dal Segno sends the instruments back to the opening violin music, and the voice falls silent. The same eight bars now carry the aria to its last fermata.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed p. 172: Dal Segno after the vocal cadence, returning to the eight-bar introduction on p. 168.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A fermata, then the alto
transitions.to: B · The alto asks for mercy
transitions.how: The violin’s eight-bar introduction closes in B minor beneath a fermata. After the pause, the alto begins “Erbarme dich”. The accompanying strings remain soft over the plucked bass; the solo violin briefly rests, then answers the voice. The rocking 12/8 pulse continues.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, vol. 4 (1854), Part II, printed pp. 168–169: B-minor cadence, fermata, alto entry and violin reply.

transitions.title: The violin carries the sentence on
transitions.from: B · The alto asks for mercy
transitions.how: The alto closes “um meiner Zähren willen” in F♯ minor and rests. Over the continuing strings and bass, the violin carries a short interlude. The voice then begins “Schaue hier”, the second part of the poem, with the same lilting metre beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed p. 170: F♯-minor cadence, violin interlude and Schaue hier.

transitions.title: Erbarme dich finds B minor again
transitions.how: The alto’s repeated “Erbarme dich” turns the music back from F♯ minor towards B minor. The bass leads the harmony home while the solo violin winds around the returning vocal phrase. Both the opening words and their key come back before the final appeal for mercy.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed pp. 171–172: repeated Erbarme dich and return of the opening text in B minor.

transitions.title: The voice leaves the violin
transitions.to: A′ · The violin has the last word
transitions.how: The alto ends “um meiner Zähren willen” with a B-minor cadence. The instruction Dal Segno returns the instruments to the opening sign: violin melody, soft string chords and plucked bass. The voice has finished. The repeated introduction closes on its original fermata.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score, printed p. 172: B-minor vocal cadence and Dal Segno; repeated introduction and fermata on p. 168.

source.title: Bach, Passionsmusik nach dem Evangelisten Matthäus (Matthäus-Passion), BWV 244, Bach-Gesellschaft Ausgabe, vol. 4, Zweiter Theil (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854)
source.locator: No. 47, Aria, printed pp. 168–172: solo violin, violins I–II, viola, alto, and organ and continuo. The strings are marked piano sempre and the bass pizzicato. Dal Segno repeats the opening violin music after the voice finishes.

timeline.note: The solo violin sings over soft string chords. Bach marks the accompanying strings piano sempre and the bass pizzicato.
The alto begins Erbarme dich after the fermata. The solo violin briefly rests, then answers her.
The alto rests while the solo violin carries an interlude above the accompanying strings and bass.
The alto returns with Schaue hier; the solo violin continues beside her.
Erbarme dich returns, with alto and violin sharing the melody above the bass.
Dal Segno brings back the opening violin music. The alto remains silent through the closing fermata.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Hertha Töpper (alto), Otto Büchner (solo violin), Münchener Bach-Orchester (orchestra), Karl Richter (conductor)
fields.note: The booklet lists Hertha Töpper for the alto arias and Otto Büchner as the violinist. The label of the LP side that carries Nos. 42–53 credits both and does not assign Büchner to a single number; his identification as this aria’s solo violinist rests on that label and on the booklet naming no other violinist. The booklet also names continuo players for the whole Passion (organ Ekkehard Tietze and Hedwig Bilgram; double bass Franz Ortner; bassoon Karl Kolbinger; viola da gamba Oswald Uhl, whom Discogs also lists on continuo cello); which of them play in this aria is not stated, so they are not listed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition is not identified. The booklet numbers the aria 47 (the Bach-Gesellschaft and BWV numbering) while the Internet Archive and retail track titles number it 39 (the New Bach Edition). The file contains the aria alone: the preceding chorus and recitative ‘Wahrlich, du bist auch einer von denen — Da hub er an’ (booklet No. 46) is the previous track and the chorale ‘Bin ich gleich von dir gewichen’ is the next. The booklet gives the composition as Leipzig 1729 or earlier, revised 1736.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 23 June – 21 August 1958 (sessions 23 June–6 July, 11–12 August and 21 August)
fields.note: The Archiv Produktion LP labels print the recording dates as 6/23–7/6, 8/11–12 and 21/1958; the retail page gives 23 June–6 July, 11–12 and 21 August 1958; the booklet essay gives 22 sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958. Which session produced this aria is not stated.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Archiv Produktion (Deutsche Grammophon Gesellschaft, History of Music Division)
fields.note: The labels read ‘Archive Production — History of Music Division Deutsche Grammophon Ges.’ and ‘Stereo’.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: SAPM 198 009/012 (first stereo edition, four LPs); the scanned export pressing carries ARC 73 125–73 128 / SAPM 198 625–628, with this aria on the side labelled ARC 73 128 b / SAPM 198 628 b
fields.note: First release year is disputed in the sources: the booklet and Wikipedia say 1959 (the booklet reads ‘LPs released/veröffentlicht/paru 1959’ and prints ℗ 1959 Deutsche Grammophon); Discogs and the Internet Archive LP catalogue give 1958, which is the recording year. Both dates precede 1963. The digital file used here is a later remaster, not the LP.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: First stereo edition: fifth programme side of the set (Discogs side E), track E6 (7:44 on the LP); matrix and take numbers not read
fields.note: The side and position come from the Discogs tracklist, whose first edition is automatically coupled, so the programme side is not the physical side of a particular LP; the scanned export label for ‘No. 42–53 Trial in the Presence of Kaiphas and Pilate (24’26)’ is numbered 5 (ARC 73 128 b / SAPM 198 628 b). No run-out inscription was seen, so matrix and take are unknown.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No remastering engineer or studio is credited in the item metadata or the booklet. The booklet’s © 2001 Deutsche Grammophon notice and the retail page’s ‘Digitally remastered’ line show only that commercial digital releases exist. The upload is a private Internet Archive upload in the hifidelity collection.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The Internet Archive item was created on 16 February 2026; that upload date is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: 24-bit/192 kHz FLAC (item description ‘1959 [FLAC 24-192]’), digitally remastered according to the retail page; streamed here through the Internet Archive’s VBR MP3 derivative.
fields.note: The item’s track titles and durations (7:46 for this track) match the retail page’s 2016 hi-res listing, so the file is probably that release, but the item names no source. No speed correction, noise reduction or restoration settings are stated.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Bach’s composition (d. 1750) and the Bach-Gesellschaft edition used for the orchestra view (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854) are public domain.
fields.note: IMSLP catalogues the Bach-Gesellschaft volume as Public Domain. This does not clear the sound recording, the later remaster or the booklet’s prose.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — European recording-rights expiry; first publication documented before 1963 (Archiv Produktion stereo LP edition, 1958 or 1959).
fields.note: Programme rule 3. The recording was made in June–August 1958 and first issued on four stereo LPs; the booklet states 1959 and quotes a critic’s review of the four LPs from May 1959. Whether the first issue fell in 1958 or 1959, a recording published by 1959 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term (to the end of 2009) before the extension that applied from 1 November 2013. This is territorial, not a licence: the Internet Archive item carries no licence URL and no Public Domain Mark. US status is not established and no US public-domain claim is made. The audio file is a later commercial digital remaster; this dossier relies on the first publication of the recording and does not separately clear any rights claimed in the remastering, which is a point for the integration lead.

composer.epithet: He supplied Leipzig’s churches with music for twenty-seven years and left keyboard players enough work for a lifetime.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, turned up in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. His cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, already makes two people say different things together: one sings the psalmist’s plea, another a hymn in long notes above it.
